svg.title: The three classes of prompt injection, ranked by blast radius
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure of three cards, each with a bar showing its blast radius. Class one, direct injection, is the user typing an instruction to ignore previous instructions; its radius is their own session, drawn shortest, and it is the kind every demo shows while being the least dangerous in production because the user is attacking themselves. Class two, indirect injection, is adversarial text arriving through a trusted channel such as a fetched web page, a seeded PDF, or a repository issue body; its radius is whatever the agent can reach, including other users' data, and it is the class that matters in production. Class three, memory poisoning, plants a fact in long-term memory that later sessions retrieve and act on; its radius is widest, spanning sessions and users on a shared store, and it is hardest to detect because it is invisible in any single trace. Captions note that everything entering the context is potentially hostile.

Everything that enters the context is potentially hostile: every fetched page, every indexed document, every tool result, every memory cell.
Classical security learned this with SQL injection in the early 2000s. The vocabulary is new; the discipline is not.
In every documented incident the untrusted content arrived through a channel the system already trusted, and the damage was done by
a capability the system already had.
